hook: A Keter-class predator that turns up near wars and disasters, told mostly through the diary of a British infantryman at the Somme in 1916. The diary opens with an eager new arrival and changes voice as the weeks pass. The imagery is frightening, but most of it stays in fog, darkness and the corner of the writer's eye.
whyItMatters: The page connects to the Seas of Orcadia hub, and its tags mark it as a period piece and military fiction as well as horror. It pairs a clinical report with a found-document diary, so the report supplies scale and history while the diary supplies fear. The soldiers in the diary already have their own folklore name for the creature, which gives the anomaly a life before the Foundation's paperwork.
thingsToNotice: Watch the diary's language wear down: entries shorten, sleep disappears, and the opening bravado drains out. The report's note that the entity becomes aware of whoever sees it, and keeps coming back for them, is the frame you need when reading the later entries. The fresh-water detail in the description looks minor but explains an odd requirement in the containment procedures. Footnotes glossing British slang let the period voice stay intact without stalling the reader.
